---
order: 2
node: AC9S7U04 n2
assumes: [AC9S4U03 n1]
unit: forces
title: Does balanced mean no forces?
introduces: [balanced-forces]
summary: Balanced forces cancel out (the net force is zero), so the motion doesn't change. The object stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed. Unbalanced forces change the motion.
language: science
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8201
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8201/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
explainPicture: { ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Push 4 N, friction 4 N: balanced, so the net force is 0 N and the motion doesn't change." }
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "Balanced forces"
  say: "Balanced forces cancel out, but they are still there."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "The box is already moving. Push 4 N forward, friction 4 N back.", say: "The moving box has four newtons of push forward and four of friction back." }
    - click: "Play"
    - wait: 1500
    - caption: { text: "Balanced: net force 0 N. The dots stay evenly spaced.", say: "The forces are balanced, so the dots stay evenly spaced." }
    - wait: 2500
    - expect: { selector: "body", contains: "speed 2 m/s" }
    - caption: { text: "Balanced doesn't mean no forces: it means no change in motion.", say: "Balanced doesn't mean no forces: it means the motion doesn't change." }
    - wait: 800
hook: "A car cruises down the highway at a steady 100 km/h, engine running. Is its engine pushing harder than the air and the road are holding it back?"
---
Last time you drew forces as arrows, and now you'll find out what those arrows tell you about how something is moving.

## Engage: the cruising car

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Most students say the forward force must be bigger for a car to keep moving; the board shows balanced forces giving steady motion."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A car drives along a straight road at a steady 100 km/h. Compare the forward force from the engine with the backward forces (air and road friction)."
  options: ["Forward force is bigger, or the car would stop", "They are equal: the forces are balanced", "There are no forces on it while it cruises", "Backward forces are bigger"]
  actual: "They are equal. At a steady speed the forces are balanced: the net force is zero, so the motion doesn't change."
```

## Explore: keep it moving

```step
stage: run
insight: "Finding the push that keeps the box at a steady speed shows balanced forces with motion, not without it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#steady", height: 640 }
check: { type: board, text: "Find a push that keeps the box moving at a steady speed for at least 3 seconds.", when: "t >= 3 and f = 0 and v > 0" }
```

The box starts moving at 3 m/s. Press **Play**, then try different pushes (**Reset** to start again). Watch the speed–time graph and the dots: evenly spaced dots mean a steady speed.

## Explain: balanced and unbalanced

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Separating 'balanced' from 'no forces', then linking balance to unchanged motion, is the hinge for Newton's first law."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "When the box moved at a steady speed, what was true?"
      options: ["The push equalled friction: balanced, net force 0", "There were no forces on it", "The push was bigger than friction"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Both arrows were still there, with the push going forward and friction pulling back.", "If the push were bigger than friction, the box would speed up, and the graph shows that it didn't."]
      explain: "Balanced forces are equal and opposite, so they're both still acting but they cancel each other out."
    hint: ["Think back to the graph when you found the steady speed. What was it doing, and what were the push and friction arrows doing at that moment?", "Look at the arrows on the board while the speed is steady, and ask whether either one has gone."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "What happens with each net force? (The box is already moving to the right.)"
      options: ["Speeds up", "Steady speed", "Slows down"]
      items:
        - ["Push 9 N, friction 6 N", "Speeds up"]
        - ["Push 6 N, friction 6 N", "Steady speed"]
        - ["Push 2 N, friction 6 N", "Slows down"]
        - ["Push 12 N, friction 6 N", "Speeds up"]
    hint: ["Compare the push with the friction for each one, and ask which is left over and which way it points.", "If you're not sure, set that push on the Explore board and watch the speed-time graph."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Balanced or unbalanced?"
      options: ["Balanced", "Unbalanced"]
      items:
        - ["A book resting on a desk", "Balanced"]
        - ["A car cruising at a steady speed", "Balanced", "A steady speed in a straight line means the forces are balanced."]
        - ["A ball speeding up as it rolls down a slope", "Unbalanced"]
        - ["A skydiver falling at a steady speed", "Balanced", "Air resistance is equal to her weight, so the forces cancel."]
        - ["A cyclist braking", "Unbalanced"]
        - ["A plane taking off down the runway", "Unbalanced"]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained why a car at a steady speed has balanced forces, even though its engine is running." }
```

## Mix it up

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Balanced forces are equal and opposite, which only makes sense once arrow length is read as the size of the force."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Looking back at force arrows: a diagram shows a 30 N push to the right and 10 N of friction to the left. How do the arrows look?"
  options: ["The push arrow is three times as long as the friction arrow, and they point opposite ways", "The two arrows are the same length", "Both arrows point to the right", "The friction arrow is longer, because friction is stronger"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "The forces are different sizes, so their arrows have to be different lengths.", "Friction acts against the push, so its arrow points the other way.", "The push is the bigger force at 30 N against 10 N, so its arrow is the longer one."]
  explain: "The length of an arrow shows the size of the force and it points the way the force acts, so a 30 N push gets an arrow three times as long as a 10 N friction force."
```

## Elaborate: the falling skydiver

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "A vertical case with motion (falling at a steady speed) tests whether students apply 'balanced means no change in motion' beyond the board's horizontal case."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#skydiver", height: 560 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "A skydiver and her gear, 100 kg (weight 980 N), fall at a steady speed. Set the air resistance.", when: "A = 980" }
    hint: ["Think about the box that kept a steady speed, and what its forces were doing at that time.", "Her weight is shown as an arrow, so slide the air resistance and let the line under the board tell you what her forces are doing."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Her forces are balanced. Is she still falling?"
      options: ["Yes, at a steady speed", "No, she has stopped in mid-air", "She is speeding up"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Balanced forces don't stop motion, but they do stop it from changing.", "She would only be speeding up if there were a net force downwards, and here there isn't."]
      explain: "This steady speed is her terminal velocity, which happens because weight and air resistance cancel and so her speed stays the same."
    hint: "Think back to the box on the track when its forces balanced, and what the graph and the dots did then."
```

## Elaborate: slowing down and stopping

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Making the box stop with friction connects unbalanced forces to slowing down and shows what friction does once motion has stopped."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#stop", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Make the moving box slow down and stop.", when: "t >= 1 and v = 0" }
    hint: ["Which of the two forces on the box would have to be bigger for its speed to fall?", "The line under the board tells you the net force and which way it points, and the graph shows what the speed does when you change the push."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Once the box has stopped, with a push of 2 N, the friction is shown as 2 N, not 6 N. Why?"
      options: ["Friction only resists as much as it needs to, up to its limit", "Friction disappears when things stop", "The board is wrong"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "There is still friction, and it matches the push so the box stays put.", "If you push gently on a heavy box that doesn't move, friction is matching your push."]
      explain: "The friction on a stationary object matches the push up to a limit, which is 6 N here, and beyond that the object starts sliding."
    hint: ["Picture pushing gently on a heavy box that doesn't budge. Is the friction on it bigger than your push, or not?", "With the box stopped, slide the push on the board and watch what the friction arrow does."]
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the cruising car with what the board showed." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- **Balanced** forces are equal and opposite: the **net force is zero**. They are still acting; they cancel.
- Balanced forces mean **no change in motion**: still objects stay still; moving objects keep a steady speed in a straight line.
- **Unbalanced** forces change the motion: the object speeds up, slows down or changes direction, the way the net force points.
- A car at a steady speed has balanced forces: the engine's push equals air resistance plus friction.

```teacher
summary: Students identify balanced and unbalanced forces and predict the
  motion, recognising that balanced forces mean no change in motion, not no
  forces (AC9S7U04, node 2, a hinge node).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 8 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds
  4 min, Wider about 5 min
goals:
  - I can tell balanced from unbalanced forces in a diagram.
  - I can explain that balanced forces mean no change in motion, not no forces.
  - I can predict the motion from a force diagram.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  trolleys and force meters. Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical`
  (default) or `wider`.


  The hinge misconception is "balanced means no forces" (and its partner,
  "moving needs a forward force"). The Explore board has motion with balanced
  forces, which is exactly the case students don't expect.


  Board notes: the box moves left and right only. Friction is fixed at its limit
  while sliding and matches the push when stationary. The board starts the box
  at 3 m/s so students can find the steady-speed push (6 N).
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. Most will choose 'forward force is bigger'."
  - "Explore: if students struggle, ask them to compare the push and friction
    numbers when the graph is flat."
  - "Explain: the first question is the checkpoint; the two sorts apply it."
  - "In your own words: the 'balanced isn't no forces' paragraph is the
    evidence."
struggle: Accepting that balanced forces give steady motion, not no motion. When
  a student says the box should stop, ask what the graph did when push equalled
  friction.
stuck:
  - see: A student says the forces are balanced so the box should stop.
    ask: What did the graph do when push equalled friction?
    fix: "It stayed flat: steady speed. Balanced forces keep the motion the same."
  - see: A student says there are no forces on the cruising car.
    ask: What is the engine doing? What is the air doing?
    fix: "Both are pushing: forward and backward. They cancel."
  - see: A student thinks the skydiver stops when forces balance.
    ask: What did the box do when its forces balanced?
    fix: It kept moving at the same speed. So does she.
stretch: A spacecraft far from any planet switches off its engine. What happens
  to its motion, and why?
support: "Give the sentence frame: 'The forces are … so the net force is … so
  the motion …'."
leads: >
  Next: unbalanced forces and changes in motion (node 3), then gravity (node 4).
  In Year 10 this becomes Newton's first law.


  In class: a trolley pulled by a force meter at constant speed (the meter
  reading equals friction); a tug of war at a standstill.
exit:
  q: A cyclist rides at a steady 20 km/h on a flat road. Are the forces on her
    balanced? Explain.
  a: "Yes: she isn't speeding up or slowing down, so her forward force equals the
    backward forces (air resistance and friction)."
explain: >
  **Balanced** forces are equal and opposite: the net force is zero. They are
  still acting; they cancel. The motion doesn't change: still stays still,
  moving keeps a steady speed.


  **Unbalanced** forces change the motion, in the direction of the net force.
```
